title: Chapter 52: Lot 41, Part 3 of 5: The Plan
html:
They made the plan around him while the needles went in.
There was nowhere else to make it. Corin could not get up, and could not talk, and nobody would make it without him. So they came into the side vault, one by one, and sat on the floor round the bench, the way people sit round a sickbed. Gideon by the blue chalk shapes. Juno on her pallet, pulled close, with her wrapped feet up. Oren on his crate in the arch, half turned, so that he could hear both the long hall and the vault. Silas standing, as always, with his arms folded, against the wall by the grating. And Lyra on her knees by the bench, holding Corin's hands.
Vespera did not stop. She did not look up. Her small blue fingers moved over his face, and the needles went in, and out, and the smell of burnt honey and cloves filled the vault, and she did not say a word about any of it.
"He can't answer," said Juno.
"He can," said Lyra.
She turned his right hand over in hers, so that his gray palm lay open against her gloved one. And she said, very low, to him, "One for yes. Two for no. Three if you need us to stop."
His gray finger moved on her palm. Once.
Yes.
She had learned it from her father. On the barge. From his finger on her palm, tapping. One and the double for heard. Two for hold. It was not the same as the drum calls. It was simpler. But it was the same idea. A hand on a hand, saying what a mouth could not.
"All right," said Lyra. "From the beginning."
There had been a letter from Remy that morning. It had come with the bread, at the eighth bell, in Bridie's basket, folded very small under the cabbage leaf with the cheese. Bridie said a boy had given it to her on the Bourse kitchen step, a boy in plum livery she had never seen before, who said for the doctor's barrow and went back in. That was the usual way. I'll send word by the usual way when I know what she's going to do with the box, Remy had said on Tuesday night. And now he knew.
Lyra had read it aloud at the eighth bell. She read it again now. For Oren. For all of them. It was very short. Remy's hand was small and neat and sloped backward, the hand of a boy who had kept books in secret since he was ten.
The box stays cold until a quarter before midnight. In the cold room under the dome. Below the floor of the hall, under the brass bid box. The third door is not a door. It is the floor. At a quarter before midnight the floor opens and the Fourth Tier lots go up on a lift into the box, so that she can take them out in front of everybody at the stroke. Lot 41 goes up last.
The glass passage knows you now. Door 3 at a quarter to. I will be on the back stair below the gallery. I will take you down. I cannot take you up.
Burn this.
R.
She had burned it, after the eighth bell. She had kept every word of it in her head.
"So," said Lyra. "The door that isn't a door is the floor. And the box is under it. And it goes up at a quarter to midnight, and Lot 41 goes up last. So there's a little time. Between a quarter to midnight and the stroke. While the other lots are going up. When it's still down there, in the cold, and everybody upstairs is looking at the brass box and waiting."
One tap on her palm.
"And you go in by door three at a quarter to," said Lyra. "With the key. The one in the mask. From the kitchen yard, up the back stair, the way the waiters go. And Remy meets you on the stair, below the gallery, and takes you down. Through the glass."
One tap.
"Down," said Silas from the wall. "Not up. He said he can't take you up."
"No," said Lyra. "He can't. So you don't come up." She looked at Gideon. "You come out."
Gideon was sitting by the chalk shapes with his knees drawn up and his carved barge in his hands, turning it over. He did not look up.
"The ring passage," he said. "Under the floor. It goes all the way round. The cold room's in the middle, under the dome. The ring goes round it, like a wheel round the hub. And there's a way from the ring to the coal cellar. On the east side. By the lift, and the stone stair to the kitchen. Past the bench where the porters sit." He turned the barge over. "I'll be on the ring. At a quarter to. With my chalk. I'll mark the way. Blue. Low down on the wall, by the floor, where nobody looks." He looked up at last. "You won't be able to see it in the dark. I know. But you'll feel it. You can feel chalk with your fingers if you go slow. And you have to go slow anyway. Because of the leg."
One tap.
"How do you get in?" said Juno.
"The chute." Gideon shrugged. "Same as last Sunday. Cinder Lane. The iron flap. Halfway along."
"Coker's on the stool."
Gideon's face did not change.
"Coker's not Coker any more," he said. "Fane took his kindness. On Tuesday. All of it. Four glasses. Mother Grue's boy Peter went past him on Wednesday and Coker kicked him. Peter's seven." He turned the barge over. "So I won't ask Coker. I'll wait till he's at the Bell. He still goes to the Bell. He goes at the ninth and sits till the eleventh, same as always. He's not kind any more, but he still likes beer." He looked at Lyra. "I'll be on the ring by the tenth. And I'll look for my cold while I wait."
Nobody said anything to that.
Look for my cold. That had been his price, a week ago. Boots, and a loaf a day for the fifth arch, and look for my cold. A jar, with a blue chalk H on it, somewhere in the Lady's cellars. Two hundred and ninety-one to three hundred and forty, Remy's book said. All his feelings. Four winters. Corin had found one, on Sunday night, H.297, and Gideon kept it inside his coat. The rest had gone north on the Monday tide.
But not all of them, Gideon said. Not all. He had counted. There had to be more.
"Then out," said Lyra. "Along the ring, east, by the chalk. To the lift. Past the porters' bench." She stopped. "The porters."
"They won't be on the bench," said Gideon. "Not at midnight. At midnight they're on the lift. Turning it. Taking the lots up." He turned the barge over. "They'll be right there. Turning the handle. Big and Saul. Right there by the way out."
Nobody said anything.
Big Gideon and Saul. His father and his uncle. Two huge silent men in the Lady's cellars, with dead gray skin on their hands, who had been dockers once, and soldiers, and had come up in the lift one day long ago and said Not the boy. Take it out of me. And the Lady had taken it out of them, and then kept on taking it out of the boy as well, for four more winters.
"They won't stop us," said Gideon. "They don't stop anything. They don't see anything. They didn't see Corin's boot last Sunday. They looked right at it." He put the barge down on the floor beside him. Carefully. "They'll just turn the handle."
One tap on Lyra's palm. Slow.
"Then the coal cellar," said Lyra. "And up the chute. Into Cinder Lane."
"I'll be in Cinder Lane," said Oren.
They all looked at him.
He had not turned round on his crate. He was still half facing the long hall, with his sword across his knees, wrapped in its sacking. He said it to the hall.
"By the chute," said Oren. "In the dark, against the wall. From the tenth bell. With this." He put his good hand on the sword. "And when he comes up out of that hole, I'll pull him out. One arm. I've done it twice this week." He was quiet a moment. "And if anybody's in that lane who shouldn't be, I'll be there first."
"There's two of the Inquisition's men in Cinder Lane," said Juno. "Wren's list said. Cinder Lane, two."
"Then there's two," said Oren.
Nobody argued with him.
"How will you know?" said Silas quietly. "When to be ready. You can't see the hall from Cinder Lane. You can't see the clocks. And you can't—" He stopped.
"Can't read a signal," said Oren. "No. Can't read a lantern. Can't read chalk. Can't read a card in a window. Can't read anything." He said it plainly. "I can hear, though. I can hear as well as I ever could."
"I'll be on the dome," said Juno.
She said it very fast, before anybody could stop her.
Lyra looked at her. At her white face, and her wrapped feet up on the fold of blanket.
"Juno—"
"There's two climbers on the dome," said Juno. "The list says. Roof, two. Two of the Inquisition's men, up there in the cold, on the leads, watching the street. They won't be watching the glass. Nobody watches the glass from outside. They'll be watching Exchange Street for carriages." Her voice went up. "I know those roofs. I know every roof on Exchange Street. I've been on the Bourse dome twice, at night, in the summer, for a dare. There's a gutter round the bottom of the glass, a big lead one, as wide as a plank, where you can lie flat and look down through the dome into the hall. You can see everything. The floor. The gallery. The brass box in the middle." She swallowed. "I'll lie in the gutter. On my front. I won't need my feet for that. I'll only need my eyes. And when the floor opens round the box, at a quarter to, I'll see it. And when it closes again, I'll see that. And when anything goes wrong, anything, I'll see it first."
"And then what?" said Silas.
Juno looked at Oren.
And out of the pocket of her boy's jacket she took a whistle. A tin whistle, small and battered, the kind the Watch constables used, on a loop of greasy string.
"I took it off a constable," she said. "In the autumn. He was drunk. He didn't miss it." She held it up. "It goes right across a street. It goes through walls. I've heard it from three roofs away." She looked at Oren's broad back. "One long, everything's all right. Two short, he's coming up. Three short, get out, now, all of you, run." She put it to her mouth, but did not blow it. "You don't have to read that. You only have to hear it."
Oren did not turn round. But his big gray head moved. Once.
"One long," he said. "Two short. Three short." He said it again, under his breath, the way Lucian counted steps. "One long. Two short. Three short." He was quiet. "I'll know it."
One tap on Lyra's palm. Then another, after a pause. And then a third.
She looked down at his gray hand in hers. Three. Stop. She looked at Vespera.
Vespera had stopped. She was sitting back on her heels with a needle in her fingers, looking at Corin's face. At his eyes, which had opened. They were wet. Not from the needles. Lyra could see that.
"He's all right," said Vespera, after a moment. "That's not the binding. Leave him."
Nobody asked what it was. Nobody needed to.
After a while his finger moved again on Lyra's palm. Once. Go on.
And Vespera bent over him again, and the needles went in, and Lyra said, quite steadily, "And me. At the front door. On the Duke's arm. In his mask."
She did not say whose mask. Everybody knew.
It was in its gray box on the end of the bench. White silk, seamless, with a seed-pearl edge, and silver thread round the eyes, and long white ribbons. And a little gray pocket over the bridge of the nose, empty now, where a brass key stamped V and 3 had been, before Corin put it inside his Ledger. And stitched into the lining, in double gold thread, the face of a clock with its hands at a quarter to midnight.
He's just seen that you didn't wear his present, the Duke had said to her on Friday night, in her aunt's long room, when the Treasurer looked at her bare face.
On Monday she would wear it.
She would walk up the steps of the Bourse on the Duke's arm in her mother's gray gown and the Treasurer's white mask, and she would let him see it, and she would let him think whatever he liked. And when the tall sour man in the gold livery with the stiff left leg poured the Duke's wine, she would touch his gloved hand once, as if by accident, so that he would know she was there. And then she would stand under the dome with five hundred people in masks, and smile, and wait for a quarter to midnight.
"I'll put a thread in it for you," said Vespera, without looking up from Corin's face. "Round the eyes, under the silver, where nobody will see it. A thread of quiet. So that nobody who reads faces can read yours." A needle went in. "Not the Inquisitor. Not that girl of his in white. Not the Treasurer. Not anybody."
"Can you do that?"
"I can do that," said Vespera. "It's a small thing. A face that doesn't move unless you tell it to." Another needle. "I did it for myself for twenty years. I know how it's done."
Lyra looked at her.
At her small sooty face, with the faint blue shadow along the jaw. At her blue hands, moving, steady, over Corin's burning face. At the tiny half-word tattooed on the inside of her left wrist, that Lyra had seen in the autumn and never asked about. HOLL—
She did not ask now either.
"Thank you," she said.
"Don't," said Vespera. "I'm doing it for nothing. I told you. I don't know how to be thanked for nothing."
The Tower
At a quarter before the sixth bell, Lyra gave Corin's hands to Gideon and went up the tower.
Nobody told her to. Silas had told her not to. Stay down here, my lady. There's nothing to see. A man sitting on a step, and some other men coming to get him. You've seen that before. You don't need to see it again. But she went. She did not know how to explain it to him. She only knew that somebody ought to see it. That it ought to be seen, properly, by somebody who knew who he was and what he was doing and why. Not just by a young man on a wall with a pie, writing it in a book.
Gideon took Corin's hands without being asked. He knelt down on the stone beside the bench where Lyra had knelt for five hours, and took the two gray hands in his own, and held them against Corin's chest, very carefully, the way he held his carved barges. He did not say anything. He did not look at Corin's face, which was swollen now, and red, and strange, and not Corin's any more. He looked at the hands.
"One for yes," Lyra told him. "Two for no. Three for stop."
"I know," said Gideon. "I was listening."
She went up through the church in the dusk. It was nearly dark inside now, the green light gone gray and thin, the faded saints on the walls only shapes. The three old women had gone home. The church was empty. She went past the font, and the back pews, and the great west door, which was shut, and through the low black oak door in the porch beside it, into the bottom of the tower.
She had been here once before. On Thursday. With Rowan. She had climbed these steps with her heart going so hard she could hear it, to meet a brother who did not trust her and whom she did not trust. She had counted them then. A hundred and four. She counted them again now.
They went up and round and round a stone pillar in the middle, like the inside of a shell, very steep and very narrow, with a thick old rope fixed to the wall on iron rings for a handrail. Every twenty steps or so there was a slit in the wall, narrow and tall, no wider than her hand, with no glass in it. The cold came in through the slits in thin knives. And a little gray light. And the sound of the city. Far away. A cart. A dog. Somebody calling a child in for supper.
At the top of the steps there was a ladder. She went up it. Through a square hole in a wooden floor. Into the clock room.
It was just as she remembered it. A square room of rough stone, not very big, with a wooden floor marked all over with the prints of boots. Hers and Rowan's, from Thursday, still there in the dust. In the middle of the room the clock. The great iron works of it, black and silent, taller than she was, all wheels and bars and teeth, as still as a dead animal. The long iron weights hung down from it on chains through holes in the floor, and did not move. The little brass dial on the wall by the window, that showed the time to anybody who climbed up here to look, said twenty past four. It had said twenty past four for longer than anybody could remember.
A place where it is always the same time, her mother had said.
And the window. Round, like a ship's window, set deep in the thick stone wall, and filled with old green bottle-glass in little thick round panes, each with a bubble in the middle like an eye. The light came through it green. Even now, at dusk, it came through green, faint and wavering, and lay on the dusty floor in a pale oval.
Above her head, through another square hole in the ceiling, she could see the bottom of the ladder that went up to the bell. And the bell itself. Or the lip of it. Green-black bronze, enormous, hanging in the dark.
Pigeons muttered somewhere up there, settling for the night.
Lyra went to the window.
One of the little round panes near the bottom was cracked, and a piece had fallen out of it long ago, leaving a gap the size of a coin. She had found it on Thursday. She put her eye to it now.
And there was Saint Bride's Lane, below her, in the snow and the dusk.
She could see all of it from up here. The front of the church, directly below. The steps, three wide stone steps going down from the great west door to the path. The path, going away between the graves to the lych gate, the little roofed gate at the edge of the churchyard, with snow on its roof. The yews, black, with snow on their branches like cloth. And beyond the lych gate, the lane itself, narrow and cobbled and white, with the black fronts of the houses opposite, and a lamp at the corner, not yet lit.
And on the low wall beside the lych gate, a young man in a gray cap.
Not the first boy. The second one. Older. Fourteen, maybe fifteen. Thin, with a long neck and a red nose, in a gray cap pulled down over his ears and a gray coat too big for him. He was sitting on the wall with his knees drawn up, the way he had been sitting all day, with a little black book open on his knees and a pencil in his hand. There was no pie now. He had finished the pie. There was only the book.
He was looking at the church door.
Lyra looked at it too. Straight down. At the top of the three stone steps. At the great west door, black oak, with its iron studs and its great iron ring. And at the four little holes in the wood, at the height of a man's face, where the clerk had nailed the notice yesterday morning and Silas had torn it down.
The door opened.
She heard it. Even from up here. The long groan of the old hinges, coming up through the stone of the tower and the floor of the clock room and into her feet.
And Silas came out.
He came out slowly, the way he did everything, ducking his head under the low lintel of the door though he did not need to. He had his old black coat on, too short in the sleeves. He had his gray waistcoat on, with the three missing buttons. He had his doctor's bag in his hand, the old black one with the brass clasp that he carried everywhere. And he had his spectacles on. Crooked. She could see that, even from up here. One lens a little higher than the other, catching the last of the gray light.
He pulled the great door shut behind him. It groaned again, and closed.
Then he stood at the top of the steps for a moment, and looked out over the churchyard. At the graves. At the yews. At the lych gate, and the young man on the wall, who had looked up from his book and gone very still.
And he sat down.
He sat down on the top step, in the snow, under the door. With his long legs folded up in front of him like a heron's, and his bag on the step beside him, and his long hands hanging between his knees. The way a man sits on his own front step on a summer evening, waiting for the cool. As if he had all the time in the world.
He did not look up at the tower. He did not look anywhere. He just sat there.
On the wall by the lych gate, the young man in the gray cap had stopped writing. He was staring. Lyra saw him look at the door, and then at Silas, and then at the door again. Then down at his book. Then at Silas. He did not seem to know what to write. As if there was no box on the form for this.
Then he wrote something. Fast. And looked up again.
Above Lyra's head, in the dark, she heard a sound. A creak. And then another. The sound of a rope moving through an iron ring. Old Amos, up in the bell chamber, with his hands on the bell rope, his deaf old head turned toward the slit in the wall that looked across the river. Watching. Waiting for the great bell of the Ministry to swing, so that he could see it swing, and pull.
Lyra put her hands over her ears.
She did not know if it would help. On Thursday she had been here when the hour struck, and it had not helped at all. The sound had come through her hands and through her head and through the floor and through her feet, and gone down and down and down into the stone, until she could not tell where it ended and she began.
Across the river, very far away, the Ministry bell began to ring.
And above her head, Saint Bride's answered it.
One.
It was like being inside a drum. Like being inside the heart of a giant. The whole tower shook. The dust jumped on the floor. The green light trembled in its oval. The pigeons went up in a great rush of wings in the dark above, and a feather came down past her face, turning.
Two.
She kept her eye to the gap in the green glass.
Three.
Down in the lane, at the far end, by the lamp at the corner, a carriage had come round the corner.
Four.
A small closed carriage. Black. No crest on the door. Two black horses. A driver in a gray cape, high on the box, with his collar up.
Five.
It came slowly along Saint Bride's Lane, in the snow, between the black fronts of the houses. It did not hurry. Its wheels left two dark lines in the white behind it.
Six.
It stopped at the lych gate.
And the sixth bell went down and down and down through the stone of the tower, through the floor, through Lyra's feet, into the ground, into the crypt, into the place where fifty-one children lay on their pallets with their eyes open watching the lamps, and was gone.
And in the silence after it, she heard the carriage door open.
